summaries.example: Imagine two clocks that never touch. One shows the right time because its own gears work that way, and the other does the same. If they were made perfectly at the start, they could keep matching without one clock pushing the other. Leibniz used a similar idea for minds and bodies: each follows its own pattern, while God makes the patterns agree.
summaries.summary: Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz was a very wide-ranging thinker who lived from 1646 to 1716. He studied old and new philosophies and tried to connect them. He argued that a true substance must be a real unity and must have its own activity. His mature theory called the smallest basic substances monads. Monads are not tiny pieces of ordinary matter; they are mind-like centers of perception and activity. Leibniz said that the things we see, such as bodies and motion, are real as well-grounded appearances that depend on these simpler substances. He also proposed that the mind and body do not push or pull each other directly. Instead, each follows its own pattern, while their patterns agree because of a harmony established by God. In thinking about knowledge, Leibniz distinguished necessary truths, such as logical truths, from facts that could have been different. He held that some ideas are innate, meaning the mind has natural abilities or tendencies for discovering them. He also said that minds contain many tiny perceptions below the level of attention. Finally, Leibniz offered arguments for God's existence and defended the view that God chose the best possible world, while acknowledging that parts of the world can appear very bad to us.
key_ideas: Leibniz was a thinker who worked in philosophy, mathematics, logic, science, law, and history.
He believed that reality is made from basic active unities called monads, not from matter alone.
He thought every fact has a reason and that God chose the best among possible worlds.
He believed minds contain many tiny perceptions, most of which we do not notice.
summaries.why_it_matters: Leibniz shows how one person can connect questions about science, mathematics, the mind, God, and the basic nature of reality. His ideas also raise lasting questions about whether the world has a reason, how minds relate to bodies, and how much of our own thinking we can notice.

summaries.summary: Leibniz's philosophy develops a unified account of logic, metaphysics, epistemology, and philosophical theology, though his views changed and became more refined over his career. He treats the Principle of Contradiction and the Principle of Sufficient Reason as central guides to reasoning. His Predicate-in-Notion Principle says that in every true affirmative proposition, the predicate is contained, in some manner, in the subject. This supports a conception of individual substance through the complete individual concept: a substance has a concept from which all its true predicates can in principle be derived. Since a genuine substance must also be a true unity and a source of activity, matter understood merely as extended and infinitely divisible cannot be substance in the strict sense. Leibniz's mature ontology therefore identifies the fundamental substances with monads: simple, mind-like unities endowed with perception and appetition. Bodies and motion are phenomena grounded in the ordered activity of monads, rather than independent substances of the Cartesian kind. Because finite substances do not causally transfer states to one another, Leibniz explains their correspondence through pre-established harmony. Each substance unfolds from its own internal law, yet its perceptions and activities match those of other substances. This supports two explanatory perspectives: efficient causes describe mechanical bodily processes, while final causes describe action in terms of ends. In epistemology, Leibniz distinguishes truths of reason, which are necessary and analyzable through concepts, from truths of fact, which are contingent but still require reasons. key_ideas: Leibniz combines Aristotelian and Scholastic themes with early modern mechanism, mathematics, and rationalism rather than simply choosing one tradition.
His logical account of substance connects truth, individuality, modality, and the idea that a substance's complete concept contains its predicates.
He rejects matter understood as extension alone because extension is divisible and does not itself supply a source of activity.
Monads are simple, active, perceptive substances; bodies are phenomena grounded in monads, not substances in the strictest sense.
The mind-body relation is explained by pre-established harmony, while bodily events and mental actions can be described through efficient and final causes respectively.
Leibniz distinguishes necessary truths from contingent truths and argues that experience cannot by itself explain necessary knowledge.
summaries.why_it_matters: Leibniz matters because he offers a highly systematic attempt to explain how logic, science, mind, and theology can fit together. His arguments invite scrutiny of assumptions that often seem obvious: that matter is fundamental, that causes must involve physical contact, that consciousness is transparent to itself, and that facts may simply be brute or unexplained. Even where one rejects his conclusions, the structure of his questions continues to shape debates about identity, possibility, causation, consciousness, and the relationship between mathematical description and metaphysical explanation.

important_terms.definition: A basic constituent of reality that has genuine unity and is capable of activity.
Leibniz's idea that a complete concept of an individual contains every predicate truly belonging to that individual, across its history.
The claim that a proposition cannot be true and false in the same respect at the same time; it also grounds identity claims.
The claim that nothing is the case without an adequate reason why it is so rather than otherwise.
The claim that no two substances can differ only numerically while sharing every intrinsic property.
Leibniz's theory that simple substances unfold independently yet correspond perfectly because God coordinated them from the beginning.
A mind-like simple substance whose perceptions and appetitions express the universe from a particular point of view.
Reflective awareness of one's own perceptions or mental states, distinguished from perception itself.

Each follows its own inner rule, while the entire performance remains matched because it was arranged in advance.
summaries.summary: Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz was a remarkably broad seventeenth- and early eighteenth-century thinker. He worked across philosophy, logic, mathematics, physics, law, history, and theology. Rather than accepting either older philosophy or modern mechanism by itself, he tried to combine insights from several traditions. His central principles include the Principle of Contradiction, the Principle of Sufficient Reason, the Principle of the Best, and the Identity of Indiscernibles. These principles help explain his account of reality. Leibniz argues that a genuine substance must be a true unity and must have an internal source of activity. A body understood only as extended matter can be divided endlessly and does not explain its own activity, so it cannot be a substance in the fullest sense. In his mature view, the basic substances are monads. Monads are simple and mind-like: they have perceptions and appetitions, or inner tendencies to move from one perception to another. They express the universe from different perspectives. The physical objects we experience are not independent substances but well-founded phenomena grounded in the organized order of monads. Leibniz denies direct causal influence between finite substances. Instead, God creates them so that their separate inner developments agree; this is pre-established harmony. The same harmony allows the mind and body to correspond without one directly pushing the other. Leibniz also distinguishes truths of reason, which are necessary and can be analyzed through concepts, from truths of fact, which are contingent but still have sufficient reasons. key_ideas: Leibniz tried to bring together ancient philosophy, Christian Platonism, Scholastic ideas, and modern science.
He argued that a real substance needs both unity and activity; matter considered only as size, shape, and motion is not enough.
Monads are the deepest realities in his mature philosophy, while ordinary bodies are well-founded phenomena based on them.
The Principle of Sufficient Reason is connected to Leibniz's view that God chose the best possible world.
He separates truths of reason from truths of fact and defends innate ideas against the blank-slate theory.
Perception comes in degrees: animals have sensation and memory, while rational minds can reflect and reason about necessary truths.
summaries.why_it_matters: Leibniz matters because he gives a powerful example of philosophy working as a connected system. His account links ideas about identity and explanation to claims about matter, minds, freedom, God, and the structure of the world. Studying him helps readers see why a seemingly simple principle—such as “everything has a reason”—can lead to difficult questions about necessity, possibility, consciousness, and whether the world could have been different.

important_terms.definition: A basic thing that exists on its own rather than merely being a feature of something else.
A basic rule saying that a statement cannot be true and false at the same time in the same way.
The rule that everything that happens has a sufficient reason for happening rather than not happening or happening differently.
Leibniz's claim that two substances cannot have all the same intrinsic properties while still being two separate things.
A complete description of an individual that includes all of that individual's true features and history.
A simple, active, mind-like substance that represents the universe from its own perspective.
Leibniz's explanation that substances do not directly cause changes in one another but still develop in perfect agreement.
Awareness of one's own thoughts or perceptions, not just having those perceptions.
